result.summary: In the 11th year of the siege, the oracle about the he-goat drinking from the Neda is read by Theoclus as a wild fig tree, so Aristomenes hides the sacred records on Mount Ithome. Then a Spartan slave herdsman, who has seduced a Messenian's wife, learns that the guards have left their posts in the rain and betrays this to his master Emperamus.

scenes.title: The oracle of the he-goat
scenes.summary: The Pythian Priestess had warned the Messenians that Messene would end when a he-goat drank from the Neda. They feared literal goats.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians face the fall of Messene as foretold by the oracle.

scenes.title: The fig tree and buried records
scenes.summary: Theoclus identifies the wild fig tree on the Neda as the he-goat. Aristomenes buries the sacred records on Mount Ithome and prays to the gods to guard them.
scenes.stakes: Losing the sacred records would mean Messene's permanent ruin and the loss of hope of return.

scenes.title: The herdsman's adultery
scenes.summary: A slave herdsman of Emperamus seduces a Messenian's wife near the Neda and visits her whenever her husband is on guard duty.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians' security is endangered by a deserter's access to their camp.

scenes.title: Rainy night and betrayal
scenes.summary: Heavy rain drives the guards from the citadel, and Aristomenes is wounded and cannot make his rounds. The herdsman overhears the husband and reveals the weakness to Emperamus.
scenes.stakes: Eira is left unguarded and could be captured by the Lacedaemonians.

alias_notes.explanation: Both mean the wild fig tree; the Messenians call it Tragus, 'He-Goat'.

notable_quotes.reason: The riddling oracle about the he-goat drinking from the Neda foretells Messene's fall.

analysis.text: Oracles are read wrongly until a wise interpreter finds their true sense, and fate cannot be avoided.
Small private failings, adultery and a neglected watch, bring down a great city, as with Troy.

language_notes.text: The Great Trench was the site of a Messenian defeat in the war against Sparta; the disaster prompted this consultation of Delphi.
"I cease to guard Messene" means the god will withdraw protection; the oracle is phrased in riddling verse, typical of Delphi.
Olynthe is a Greek name for the wild fig; Tragus means he-goat, so the Messenian dialect name makes the riddle work.
Arcana are secrets or hidden sacred things; here, the sacred records kept for Messene's future.
"Keep her under" means keep Messene subjugated permanently.
Refers to Paris's seduction of Helen, which brought the Trojan War and Troy's destruction.
Eira is the mountain stronghold where the Messenians made their last stand against Sparta; the Neda is a river nearby.
Laconia is the territory of Sparta; 'Lacedæmonians' is another name for the Spartans.
'Improvised fortifications' means hastily built defences, lacking proper battlements (parapets) or turrets (small towers).
Cephallenia is an Ionian island; Apteræan bowmen came from Aptera in Crete, serving as Spartan mercenaries.
The wife hides the herdsman and over-welcomes her husband to avert suspicion.
'Paramour' means a lover in an illicit affair.

context_notes.text: Eira was the Messenian mountain stronghold held against Sparta in the Second Messenian War, led by Aristomenes.
The Pythian Priestess was the priestess of Apollo at Delphi, who delivered oracles in his name.
Mount Ithome was the Messenians' sacred citadel mountain, with a shrine of Zeus of Ithome; the Lacedæmonians are the Spartans.
Emperamus is a Spartan of note; the herdsman is his slave, so his desertion is a slave's flight to the Messenians.
Aristomenes is the Messenian leader and hero of the Second Messenian War, whose nightly rounds kept the guards alert.
Spartan kings normally led armies, so a commander other than the kings leading the siege is notable.

literary_notes.text: The oracle hides its meaning in a seemingly absurd image, so the Messenians misread it literally.
The Messenians fear real goats while the narrator tells us the god meant something else entirely.
The tree bends and touches the water as if drinking, making the oracle's image visible.
The buried records stand for Messene's identity and its hope of return from exile.
Comparing the Messenians' fall to Troy's lends the episode epic weight and frames private desire as a cause of public ruin.
The storm and the lack of defences hint that the guards' carelessness will prove disastrous.
The husband confides the secret to his wife, unaware that her hidden lover hears it; the reader sees the danger he cannot.
